```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# gstat estimates the autocorrelation range that sizes the blocks, and ggplot2
# draws the folds and the curves. Both are Suggests, so every chunk is gated
# on them and R CMD build succeeds without either.
# `eval` gates chunks only: knitr does not apply it to inline `r ...` code,
# which runs regardless. An inline reference to something a chunk defines
# has to guard itself, as in `r if (runs) x else NA`, and so does a fig.alt
# built from the output, or the article fails to build where a package is
# missing.
has_gstat  <- requireNamespace("gstat",   quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
runs <- has_gstat && has_ggplot

# A reading written inline as code, "matched" in backticks. Inline code cannot
# hold a backtick, so the helper writes it as \x60.
as_code <- function(x) sprintf("\x60\"%s\"\x60", x)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo      = TRUE,
  message   = FALSE,
  warning   = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%",
  eval      = runs
)
```

```{r missing-deps, echo=FALSE, eval=!runs, results='asis'}
cat("*`gstat` or `ggplot2` is not installed, so the code below is shown but",
    "not run. Install them with `install.packages(c(\"gstat\", \"ggplot2\"))`",
    "and rebuild.*\n")
```

*This article needs two optional packages: `gstat` for the autocorrelation
range and `ggplot2` for the figures.*

## What a cross-validated error measures

A random fold puts a held-out point's neighbours in the training set. When the
field is spatially autocorrelated, those neighbours carry the held-out point's
value, and a model that draws on nearby observations uses them. The
cross-validation score then measures the error of predicting among the samples.
Blocks hold out whole areas, and their score measures the error of predicting
into an unsampled gap the size of a block (Roberts et al. 2017).

A cross-validated error is the error at the distance the folds put between the
held-out points and their training data. It reads low for a map whose locations
sit farther from the data than that, and high for one whose locations sit
closer.

## A learner and a simulated field

Each function that scores a model takes the folds from `make_folds()` through
its `folds` argument: `cv_rf()`, `cv_gwr()` and `cv_bayes()` for the built-in
backends, `compare_models_cv()` to score several on the same folds, and
`cv_spatial()` for a learner of your own. This article uses a
five-nearest-neighbour smoother written for `cv_spatial()`. It needs no
optional package and predicts from the five nearest observations alone, so how
far the folds hold those observations away decides its score.

```{r learner}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

knn_fit <- function(train_sf, response_var = "z", k = 5L) {
  new_spatial_fit(
    subclass       = "knnsurf_fit",
    engine         = list(xy = st_coordinates(train_sf),
                          y = st_drop_geometry(train_sf)[[response_var]],
                          k = k),
    formula        = as.formula(paste(response_var, "~ 1")),
    response_var   = response_var,
    predictor_vars = character(0),
    data_sf        = train_sf
  )
}

predict.knnsurf_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
  e  <- object$engine
  xy <- if (is.null(newdata)) e$xy else st_coordinates(newdata)
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(xy)), function(i) {
    d <- sqrt((e$xy[, 1] - xy[i, 1])^2 + (e$xy[, 2] - xy[i, 2])^2)
    mean(e$y[order(d)[seq_len(min(e$k, length(d)))]])
  }, numeric(1))
}
registerS3method("predict", "knnsurf_fit", predict.knnsurf_fit)

knn_fn <- function(train_sf, ...) knn_fit(train_sf, "z", k = 5L)
```

`cv_spatial()` needs only the constructor and a `predict()` method.
`?new_spatial_fit` lists what `summary()` and `model_metrics()` need on top of
that, and `vignette("models")` explains the pattern.

The data are 400 points in a 1,000 m square (EPSG:32632) over a simulated
exponential field with scale 60 m, whose effective range is three times that,
180 m. The `sd = 0.3` term adds measurement noise.

```{r fixture}
set.seed(7)
n  <- 400
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 60) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
        rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
pts  <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
```

## Random folds against blocks

The next chunk scores the same learner on the same data with random folds and
with blocks, and prints the size of the blocks built.

```{r the-gap}
fr <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fb <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 200, seed = 1)
c(width = fb$params$block_width, height = fb$params$block_height)

cv_random  <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = fr)
cv_blocked <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = fb)

c(random  = cv_random$overall$RMSE,
  blocked = cv_blocked$overall$RMSE,
  ratio   = cv_blocked$overall$RMSE / cv_random$overall$RMSE)
```

`block_size` is the smallest edge a block may have. `make_folds()` fits a whole
number of blocks across each axis, so over this square `block_size = 200`
builds a `r if (runs) fb$params$grid_nx else NA` by
`r if (runs) fb$params$grid_ny else NA` grid of blocks
`r if (runs) round(fb$params$block_width) else NA` m wide and
`r if (runs) round(fb$params$block_height) else NA` m tall, wider than the
180 m range. "Choosing a block size" below sizes the blocks from the data.
Without `folds`, `cv_spatial()` builds block folds itself; build them with
`make_folds()` when you want to inspect or reuse them.

Blocked folds put the error
`r if (runs) round(100 * (cv_blocked$overall$RMSE / cv_random$overall$RMSE - 1)) else NA`
percent higher on this fixture. Both numbers come from the same 400
observations and the same smoother; only the fold assignment differs.

Two choices made outside the folds change what either score measures. A model
given the coordinates as predictors (`fit_rf_model(include_coords = TRUE)`) can
learn the training surface by location, so its error grows quickly with the
distance from the data. Predictors chosen on the whole data set have seen every
held-out row, and `select_features_forward()` chooses them inside the folds
instead. `vignette("models")` covers both.

## Which score matches your map

The number that applies depends on where the map predicts. `fold_separation()`
takes the locations the map will predict at and compares two sets of
distances: from each of those locations to the nearest training point, and
from each held-out point to the nearest point of its fold's training data.
Here the map is a 30 by 30 grid of points over the square, and `reading()`
returns the one-word reading of a set of folds against it.

```{r separation}
map_pts <- st_make_grid(pts, n = c(30, 30), what = "centers")

reading <- function(folds, data = pts) {
  sep <- fold_separation(folds, data, prediction_points = map_pts)
  attr(sep, "target")$reading
}
c(random = reading(fr), blocked = reading(fb))
```

The reading is one of four:

- `"matched"`: the held-out points sit about as far from their training data
  as the map's points do, so the score estimates the error at the map's
  distances.
- `"farther"`: they sit farther, and the score tends to read high for this map.
- `"closer"`: they sit closer, and the score tends to read low for this map.
  Random folds on clustered samples, with a map of the whole region, read this
  way.
- `"mixed"`: closer at some distances and farther at others, so the distances
  give no single direction.

The reading compares nearest-neighbour distances only. On clustered samples, a
learner that averages several neighbours can still score low when those
distances match.

`print()` gives the distances fold by fold:

```{r separation-print}
sep_blocked <- fold_separation(fb, pts, prediction_points = map_pts)
sep_blocked
```

`min_dist` and `median_dist` run from each held-out point to its nearest
training point, `target` is the median distance from the map's points to the
same training data, and `gap` is the fold's mean held-out distance minus its
mean prediction distance. The lines under the table pool the folds: the
held-out points sit a median of
`r if (runs) round(attr(sep_blocked, "target")$held_out_median, 1) else NA` m
from their training data, and the map's points
`r if (runs) round(attr(sep_blocked, "target")$target_median, 1) else NA` m.

### Clustered samples

The points of this fixture cover the square evenly, so random folds read
`r if (runs) as_code(reading(fr)) else NA` for a map of it. The next
chunk keeps only the points within 120 m of six of them, a clustered sample,
and reads random folds and kNNDM folds against the same map of the whole
square.

```{r clustered}
set.seed(2)
centres <- pts[sample(nrow(pts), 6), ]
cl <- pts[lengths(st_is_within_distance(pts, centres, dist = 120)) > 0, ]
nrow(cl)

fr_cl <- make_folds(cl, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fk_cl <- make_folds(cl, k = 5, method = "knndm", prediction_points = map_pts,
                    seed = 1)
c(random = reading(fr_cl, cl), knndm = reading(fk_cl, cl))

cv_random_cl <- cv_spatial(cl, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                           folds = fr_cl)
cv_knndm_cl  <- cv_spatial(cl, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                           folds = fk_cl)
c(random = cv_random_cl$overall$RMSE, knndm = cv_knndm_cl$overall$RMSE)
```

```{r clustered-text, include=FALSE}
sep_cl <- attr(fold_separation(fr_cl, cl, prediction_points = map_pts),
               "target")
```

Random folds read `r if (runs) as_code(reading(fr_cl, cl)) else NA`:
each held-out point keeps training points from its own cluster, a median of
`r if (runs) round(sep_cl$held_out_median, 1) else NA` m away, while the
map's points sit a median of
`r if (runs) round(sep_cl$target_median, 1) else NA` m from the same
training data. `method = "knndm"` (Linnenbrink et al. 2024) builds `k` folds
whose held-out distances come as close as it can to the distances from
`map_pts` to the samples, here by grouping the samples into
`r if (runs) fk_cl$params$n_clusters else NA` clusters, and reads `r if (runs) as_code(reading(fk_cl, cl)) else NA`. Its RMSE of
`r if (runs) round(cv_knndm_cl$overall$RMSE, 2) else NA`, against
`r if (runs) round(cv_random_cl$overall$RMSE, 2) else NA` for random folds, is
the score at the distances the map has to reach. For this five-neighbour
learner it can still read low for this map, as the caveat on clustered samples
above says.

## The six fold schemes

`make_folds(method = )` builds six fold schemes:

| `method` | held out in each fold | also left out of training | needs | suits a map that |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `random_kfold` | a random 1/k of the rows | nothing | `k` | predicts among the samples, over an area they cover evenly |
| `block_kfold` | the points in whole blocks of a grid, or of `blocks` | nothing | `k`; optionally `block_size`, `auto_range`, `block_nx`/`block_ny` or `blocks` (otherwise about `block_multiplier * k` blocks) | predicts into unsampled gaps about as wide as the blocks |
| `buffered_loo` | one point | every point within `buffer` of it | `buffer`; `max_test` limits the number of fits | predicts at a known distance from the data |
| `leave_location_out` | every row of one or more locations | nothing | `group_var` | predicts at sites with no measurements, from repeated measurements at others |
| `nndm` | one point | neighbours, chosen to match the prediction distances (Milà et al. 2022) | `prediction_points`; at most 5,000 rows | predicts at known locations, with a model cheap enough to refit once per point |
| `knndm` | one of `k` folds, from clusters of the points or a random partition, whichever comes closer to the prediction distances | nothing | `prediction_points` | predicts at known locations, from a larger layer or with a costly model |

```{r alt-folds, include=FALSE}
per_fold <- range(lengths(fb$params$fold_blocks))
alt_folds <- sprintf(paste(
  "A square study area divided into a %d by %d grid of blocks, with the points",
  "coloured by fold and the axes in metres of EPSG:32632. Every block belongs",
  "to one fold, and each fold is %d to %d blocks spread over the square."),
  fb$params$grid_nx, fb$params$grid_ny, per_fold[1], per_fold[2])
```

`plot_folds()` draws the assignment, with the blocks behind it when the scheme
has any:

```{r plot-folds, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt=if (runs) alt_folds else NULL}
plot_folds(fb, pts)
```

Check whether any fold is a thin sliver or a single corner. If one is, change
the block design: a different `block_size`, or polygons of your own through
`make_folds(blocks = )`.

The next chunk runs three more schemes on the same data: kNNDM matched to the
map's points; buffered leave-one-out with a buffer of 180 m, the field's
effective range, scored on 50 of the points through `max_test`; and blocks
taken from Voronoi cells around 16 k-means seeds in place of the grid.
`leave_location_out` needs repeated measurements at the same sites, which this
fixture does not have.

```{r more-schemes}
fk   <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "knndm", prediction_points = map_pts,
                   seed = 1)
floo <- make_folds(pts, method = "buffered_loo", buffer = 180, max_test = 50,
                   seed = 1)
vor  <- build_tessellation(voronoi_seeds_kmeans(pts, 16), quiet = TRUE)
fv   <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", blocks = vor$cells,
                   seed = 1)

schemes <- list(knndm = fk, buffered_loo = floo, voronoi_blocks = fv)
data.frame(
  folds   = sapply(schemes, function(f) f$k),
  reading = sapply(schemes, reading),
  RMSE    = sapply(schemes, function(f)
    cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = f)$overall$RMSE)
)
```

kNNDM keeps the random partition here (`fk$params$chosen` is
`r if (runs) as_code(fk$params$chosen) else NA`), as it does for samples
spread evenly over the map. The 180 m buffer and the Voronoi blocks, about
`r if (runs) round(fv$params$block_scale) else NA` m across, both hold the
held-out points farther from their training data than the map's points sit.
`make_folds(blocks = )` takes any polygons of your own the same way, such as
the cells of another tessellation or a set of watersheds.

## Choosing a block size

Make the blocks as wide as the gaps the map has to bridge. The wider the
blocks, the farther the held-out points sit from their training data, and the
score is the error at that distance.

### From the autocorrelation range

The autocorrelation range is the distance beyond which an observation says
little about a location. Using it as the smallest block edge is one way to
choose the separation, and suits a map that has to reach that far from the data
(Roberts et al. 2017; Valavi et al. 2019).

```{r sac}
sac <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z")
c(range  = as.numeric(sac),
  nugget = sac_nugget(sac),
  sill   = sum(attr(sac, "variogram_model")$psill))
```

The estimated range, `r if (runs) round(as.numeric(sac), 1) else NA` m, is
close to the 180 m the field was simulated with. `sac_nugget()` reads the
nugget off the same fitted model; here it is
`r if (runs) round(100 * sac_nugget(sac) / sum(attr(sac, "variogram_model")$psill)) else NA`
percent of the sill. A nugget that is most of the sill means nearby
observations carry little information, and the blocked and random scores tend
to be close.

```{r alt-sac, include=FALSE}
alt_sac <- sprintf(paste(
  "Empirical variogram of z: semivariance against distance in metres, with",
  "points sized by the number of point pairs, a fitted curve that levels off",
  "near %.2f, and a dotted vertical line at the effective range of %.1f m."),
  sum(attr(sac, "variogram_model")$psill), as.numeric(sac))
```

`plot()` draws the variogram behind the estimate:

```{r plot-sac, fig.height=4, fig.alt=if (runs) alt_sac else NULL}
plot(sac)
```

The points are the empirical semivariances, sized by the number of point pairs
behind each, the curve is the fitted model, and the dotted line marks the
effective range given in the subtitle. When no range is identified, the
subtitle gives the reason and no line is drawn.

`make_folds(auto_range = TRUE)` runs this estimate and uses it as the smallest
block edge:

```{r auto-range}
fa <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", response_var = "z",
                 auto_range = TRUE, seed = 1)
c(range  = as.numeric(fa$params$sac_range),
  width  = fa$params$block_width,
  height = fa$params$block_height)
```

The blocks are a little wider than the range because a whole number of them
has to fit across the square.

When the variogram identifies no range, `estimate_sac_range()` returns `NA`
with the reason attached. `auto_range` then warns and falls back to the default
grid, about `block_multiplier * k` blocks over the extent (15 at `k = 5`), and
you are back to choosing a size yourself. `?estimate_sac_range` lists each
reason and what it means, and `plot()` draws the variogram wherever one was
computed.

### The error at each block size

`cv_block_size_sweep()` runs the cross-validation at several block sizes and
reports the curve, with a random-fold run as the reference. Each size is a full
cross-validation, so five sizes at `k = 5` make 25 fits, plus 5 for the random
reference; `max_fits` caps that.

```{r sweep}
sw <- cv_block_size_sweep(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                          k = 5, n_sizes = 5, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
sw
```

```{r alt-sweep, include=FALSE}
sw_df  <- data.frame(sw)
sw_blk <- sw_df[!is.na(sw_df$block_size), ]
alt_sweep <- sprintf(paste(
  "Cross-validated RMSE against the smallest block edge asked for, in metres",
  "on a log scale. The error rises from %.2f at %.0f m to %.2f at %.0f m,",
  "above the dashed random-fold reference of %.2f. A shaded band gives the",
  "range across folds at each size, and a dotted line marks the estimated",
  "autocorrelation range of %.0f m."),
  sw_blk$value[1], sw_blk$block_size[1],
  sw_blk$value[nrow(sw_blk)], sw_blk$block_size[nrow(sw_blk)],
  sw_df$value[is.na(sw_df$block_size)], attr(sw, "sac_range"))
```

```{r plot-sweep, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt=if (runs) alt_sweep else NULL}
plot(sw)
```

The error climbs away from the random-fold reference as the blocks widen, and
the dotted line marks the estimated range. Each point of the curve is the
error of a map whose locations sit as far from the data as that size's held-out
points do. To choose a size, run `fold_separation()` on the folds of each size,
the `$folds` of each element of `attr(sw, "results")`, against the map's
points. `block_size` is the smallest edge asked for and `block_width` the edge
built:

```{r sweep-separation}
sizes <- data.frame(sw)[, c("block_size", "block_width", "value")]
sizes$reading <- sapply(attr(sw, "results"), function(r) reading(r$folds))
sizes
```

```{r sweep-text, include=FALSE}
blk      <- !is.na(sizes$block_size)
matched  <- blk & sizes$reading == "matched"
largest  <- which.max(sizes$block_size)
```

For a map of this square the random folds read
`r if (runs) as_code(sizes$reading[!blk][1]) else NA`, and so do the
blocks asked for at
`r if (runs) paste(round(sizes$block_size[matched], 1), collapse = ", ") else NA`
m. Their scores,
`r if (runs) paste(round(sizes$value[!blk | matched], 2), collapse = " and ") else NA`,
are the errors at the map's distances; the larger sizes read
`r if (runs) as_code(unique(sizes$reading[blk & !matched])) else NA`.

Watch `blocks_used` as the blocks grow. At the largest size,
`r if (runs) round(sizes$block_size[largest], 1) else NA` m asked for and
`r if (runs) round(sizes$block_width[largest], 1) else NA` m built,
`r if (runs) sw_df$blocks_used[largest] else NA` blocks hold the points for
`r if (runs) sw_df$k[largest] else NA` folds, so each fold holds out a large
piece of the square. That score is the error of a map that has to reach across
such a piece.

## Reading a cross-validation result

`overall` is the pooled score and `fold_metrics` has one row per fold.

### Spread across folds

```{r alt-metrics, include=FALSE}
fold_rmse <- cv_blocked$fold_metrics$RMSE
alt_metrics <- sprintf(paste(
  "RMSE for each of %d folds, with point size showing how many rows each held",
  "out. The values run from %.2f to %.2f around a dashed pooled line at %.2f."),
  length(fold_rmse), min(fold_rmse), max(fold_rmse),
  cv_blocked$overall$RMSE)
```

`plot_cv_metrics()` shows the spread across folds. A pooled RMSE built from one
catastrophic fold and four good ones describes neither; here the five blocked
folds run from `r if (runs) round(min(fold_rmse), 2) else NA` to
`r if (runs) round(max(fold_rmse), 2) else NA`.

```{r plot-metrics, fig.height=4, fig.alt=if (runs) alt_metrics else NULL}
plot_cv_metrics(cv_blocked, metric = "RMSE")
```

### Folds and rows accounted for

Two counts and four fields say what happened on the way through:
`n_folds_attempted` against `n_folds_succeeded`; `fold_status`, one row per
fold; `n_dropped`, rows removed for a missing or non-finite value;
`orphan_rows`, rows no fold names; and `n_unknown_ids`, row IDs the folds name
that the data do not have. On the clean run above nothing went missing:

```{r accounting-clean}
c(attempted = cv_blocked$n_folds_attempted,
  succeeded = cv_blocked$n_folds_succeeded,
  dropped   = cv_blocked$n_dropped,
  orphans   = length(cv_blocked$orphan_rows),
  unknown   = cv_blocked$n_unknown_ids)
```

The next three runs each lose something: a learner that fails on one fold,
data with three missing values scored on folds built on the first 300 rows,
and the first 300 rows scored on folds built on all 400.

### Folds that failed

The next chunk scores a learner that fails on one fold.

```{r failing-fold, warning=TRUE}
flaky <- function(train_sf, ...) {
  if (nrow(train_sf) < 320) stop("not enough training rows for this learner")
  knn_fit(train_sf, "z", k = 5L)
}
cv_flaky <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = flaky, folds = fb)

cv_flaky$fold_status
c(attempted = cv_flaky$n_folds_attempted,
  succeeded = cv_flaky$n_folds_succeeded)
```

`fold_status` names every fold supplied and what became of it, with the error
text for the ones that failed. `status` is one of `ok`, `error`, `skipped`,
`dropped` or `worker_error`. `overall` then pools the
`r if (runs) cv_flaky$n_folds_succeeded else NA` folds that ran,
`r if (runs) nrow(cv_flaky$predictions) else NA` of the 400 rows, and
`cv_spatial()` warns about it, since a fold that fails is often the hardest one
to predict. `fold_status` keeps each cause with the result, so a script or a
knitted report still has it after the console output is gone.

### Rows left out

```{r accounting, warning=TRUE}
holed <- pts
holed$z[c(3, 17, 42)] <- NA                       # three rows will be dropped
part  <- make_folds(pts[1:300, ], k = 4, method = "block_kfold", seed = 1)

cv_acc <- cv_spatial(holed, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = part)

c(n_dropped     = cv_acc$n_dropped,
  n_orphans     = length(cv_acc$orphan_rows),
  n_unknown_ids = cv_acc$n_unknown_ids)
```

`n_dropped` is how many rows `prep_model_data()` removed for a missing or
non-finite value before any fold was fitted. `orphan_rows` holds the row IDs no
fold names, which here is rows 301 to 400, because the folds were built on the
first 300. `n_unknown_ids` counts the distinct row IDs the folds name that the
data do not have, which here is the three rows the `NA`s removed.

The two mirror each other, and which one is non-zero tells you which way the
mismatch runs:

```{r mirror}
cv_rev <- cv_spatial(pts[1:300, ], "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                     folds = fb)
c(n_orphans = length(cv_rev$orphan_rows), n_unknown_ids = cv_rev$n_unknown_ids)
```

Folds built on more rows than the data has give `n_unknown_ids`; folds built on
fewer give `orphan_rows`. Rows in `orphan_rows` are never scored, so the score
covers every observation only when `orphan_rows` is empty, no row was dropped
and every fold ran. Unknown IDs cost the folds rows but leave every
observation scored: the run above predicts
`r if (runs) nrow(cv_rev$predictions) else NA` of its 300 rows.

## Interval calibration (Bayesian GP)

A Bayesian GP predicts an interval for each held-out value, and a calibration
check compares the share of values each interval contains with the share it
claims. `plot_calibration()` draws, for each nominal level, the share of held-out
values the intervals contained, pooled and fold by fold, from a `cv_bayes()`
result. The chunk below is not run here, because it needs `brms` and a Stan
toolchain and takes minutes. Nine coverage levels give a curve in place of the
default three.

```{r calibration, eval=FALSE}
cvb <- cv_bayes(pts, "z", character(0), folds = fb,
                coverage_levels = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1),
                fit_args = list(chains = 2, iter = 1000))
plot_calibration(cvb)
```

Points below the diagonal are intervals that are too narrow: an 80 percent
interval that contains 60 percent of the held-out values claims more certainty
than the model has.

cross-validation. This article relied on `?make_folds`, `?fold_separation`,
`?plot_folds`, `?estimate_sac_range`, `?sac_nugget`, `?cv_block_size_sweep`,
`?cv_spatial`, `?new_spatial_fit`, `?plot_cv_metrics` and `?plot_calibration`.
`vignette("glossary")` defines the terms it uses.
